newsitem.title: UK: Oil tumbles as investment funds join sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Oil tumbles as investment funds join sell-off.

text.p: World oil markets, suffering a severe case of vertigo, steadied themselves on Friday after dealers bid farewell to the storming bull run which recently took crude to six-year highs.
Bellwether North Sea Brent crude dumped 90 cents on Thursday and has slipped more than $2 in two weeks -- but still stands $5 higher than at the same time a year ago.
But most remained wary of predicting any further collapse, given oil's sensitivity to low stocks approaching winter.
London December Brent futures on Friday by 1600 GMT traded up one cent at $22.70 a barrel.
Dealers said the market tumbled this week as investment funds took the view that prices were unlikely to stage a quick return to the $25.06 mid-October peak.
Oil joined gold, grain and copper as victim of an across-the-board switch by speculative money into equity and bond markets.
"The bulls have taken a serious blow," said analyst Charles Gray at brokerage Prudential Bache.
Gray said important technical markers for investment funds were swept away as dealers decided inventories of heating oil in the United States were on the mend.
Low heating oil stocks have underpinned oil prices since the summer amid concerns over possible shortages this winter.
But U.S. refinery heating oil output hit record levels last week and data from the American Petroleum Institute (API) showed a significant build in stocks.
API president Charles DiBona said on Thursday that worries over low stocks had been overdone.
Heating oil stocks, however, are still running well below normal levels for the time of year in both the U.S. and Europe and few expect crude to slip quickly back below $20.
"I don't think we can write this market off yet -- it's far too early in the winter," said Russell Hill, senior crude trader at Austrian oil company OMV in London.

"Considering that the heating oil season has barely started, the probability of stocks testing new lows during the winter is high, especially if winter-related demand gets a boost similar to last year's," said Washington-based consultancy Petroleum Finance.

"In fact, prices will remain high this winter, and heating oil markets will eventually face additional price spikes in case of cold weather, or some disruption in refinery output," Petroleum Finance said in a report.
News on Thursday that two rival Kurdish factions had agreed to extend a U.S.-brokered ceasefire in northern Iraq helped to undermine the oil market.
In Ankara, U.S. envoy Robert Pelletreau said rival Kurdish groups had agreed to extend a ceasefire in northern Iraq with a view to making it permanent.
A U.N. oil-for-food exchange was suspended at the end of August when clashes made it unsafe for U.N. monitors in the region.
Dealers still don't expect any early move to put the deal back on track, partly because the United States insists the whole package must be renegotiated.
"I suppose this puts oil-for-food back on the map but that's not the real reason this market came off," said a dealer in London.
"Basically the market lost its nerve."
